clinicalScope: Necrosis – irreversible cell death in tissues of patients of all ages, with emphasis on patterns common in low‑resource East African hospitals (e.g., ischemic renal tubular necrosis, gangrenous limb, tuberculous caseous necrosis).
title: Necrosis
subject: Pathology
summary: Necrosis is a form of uncontrolled cell death that destroys tissue architecture and triggers inflammation. It occurs when cells suffer severe injury that cannot be repaired, leading to loss of membrane integrity and release of intracellular contents.

sections.p: Necrosis is irreversible cell injury resulting in loss of plasma membrane integrity, cytoplasmic swelling, and uncontrolled release of intracellular enzymes that provoke inflammation. It is classified by the predominant tissue response and the underlying cause.
b: Coagulative – preserves outline; typical of ischemic infarcts in heart, kidney, spleen.
Liquefactive – tissue becomes liquid; seen in brain infarcts and abscesses.
Caseous – cheese‑like; hallmark of tuberculous granulomas.
Gangrenous – dry (coagulative) or wet (superimposed infection) loss of limb tissue.
Fat – saponification after pancreatitis or trauma.
Fibrinoid – immune complex deposition in vessel walls.

sections.p: Necrosis results from severe exogenous insults that overwhelm cellular defenses. In low‑resource settings, infectious, vascular, and toxic causes dominate.
b: Ischemia/hypoxia – arterial occlusion, severe anemia, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion.
Toxins – aminoglycosides, contrast media, herbal nephrotoxins, black‑water fever (malaria).
Infection – bacterial abscesses, tuberculous granulomas, necrotising fasciitis.
Mechanical pressure – prolonged obstructed labour causing obstetric fistula, crush injuries.
Inflammatory immune reactions – vasculitis, rheumatic fever affecting vessels.

sections.p: The cascade from injury to necrosis follows predictable cellular events that culminate in inflammation.
b: Severe ATP depletion → failure of Na⁺/K⁺ pump → cellular swelling.
Calcium influx activates phospholipases, proteases, and endonucleases.
Lysosomal membrane rupture releases hydrolytic enzymes.
Plasma membrane rupture → leakage of DAMPs (damage‑associated molecular patterns).
DAMPs recruit neutrophils/macrophages → inflammatory response and further tissue damage.

sections.p: Visible changes depend on the necrosis type and organ involved.
b: Coagulative – pale, firm, sharply demarcated infarct; retains tissue architecture.
Liquefactive – soft, yellow‑white pus‑filled cavity; often with gas bubbles.
Caseous – friable, white‑gray cheese‑like mass within granuloma.
Gangrenous – dry: black, shriveled; wet: moist, foul‑smelling, bulging.
Fat – chalky white nodules, often with a gritty feel.

sections.p: Histology reveals characteristic nuclear and cytoplasmic alterations.
b: Eosinophilic, glassy cytoplasm due to loss of RNA and protein denaturation.
Nuclear changes: pyknosis (shrinkage), karyorrhexis (fragmentation), karyolysis (fading).
Inflammatory infiltrate – neutrophils early, macrophages later.
Pattern‑specific features: ghost cells in coagulative necrosis; cystic spaces with necrotic debris in liquefactive necrosis.

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the organ involved and the inflammatory response.
b: Renal ATN – oliguria, rising creatinine, flank pain, possible uremic symptoms.
Limb gangrene – severe pain initially, followed by numbness, black discoloration, loss of pulses.
Brain liquefaction – focal neurological deficits, seizures, rapid deterioration.
Tuberculous caseous necrosis – chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, cavitary lesions on chest X‑ray.
Abdominal fat necrosis – epigastric pain, peripancreatic fat saponification seen on CT.

t.b: Assess renal function and detect ATN; rising creatinine >0.3 mg/dL within 48 h indicates acute kidney injury.
Detect arterial occlusion causing limb ischemia; absent flow confirms risk of gangrene.
Identify cavitary lesions (liquefactive necrosis) or caseous granulomas.
Confirms necrosis type by nuclear and cytoplasmic changes.

sections.p: Severity is staged by extent of tissue loss and systemic response.
b: Stage I – localized necrosis, no systemic inflammatory response.
Stage II – necrosis >10 % organ mass or early SIRS (temperature >38 °C or <36 °C, HR >90).
Stage III – extensive necrosis with organ failure (e.g., oliguria, altered mental status).
Stage IV – multi‑organ failure, high mortality; requires intensive support.

sections.p: Complications arise from both local tissue loss and systemic inflammation.
b: Sepsis/SIRS – release of bacterial toxins or DAMPs.
Secondary infection – wet gangrene, abscess formation.
Permanent loss of function – chronic kidney disease after ATN, limb amputation.
Fistula formation – obstetric pressure necrosis leading to vesicovaginal fistula.
Higher mortality in Stage III–IV necrosis, especially with HIV or malnutrition.

sections.p: Management targets the underlying cause, limits tissue spread, and supports organ function.
b: Remove precipitating factor – revascularize limb, stop nephrotoxic drugs, treat infection with appropriate antibiotics.
Supportive care – fluid resuscitation for ATN, analgesia, wound care for gangrene.
Surgical debridement or amputation when necrotic tissue is non‑viable or infected.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) for suspected bacterial necrosis; narrow once cultures return.
Adjunctive measures – hyperbaric oxygen for refractory gas gangrene, antitubercular therapy for caseous necrosis.

sections.p: Linking morphology to bedside findings guides decision‑making.
b: Coagulative necrosis → pale, firm infarct → correlates with sudden loss of pulse and pain‑free black limb (dry gangrene).
Liquefactive necrosis → pus‑filled cavity → presents as foul‑smelling sputum, fever, and radiologic cavitation.
Caseous necrosis → chronic constitutional symptoms + chest X‑ray cavity with irregular walls.
Fat necrosis → elevated serum lipase, CT showing fat stranding, palpable gritty nodules.

sections.p: A systematic strategy ensures you capture key clues and avoid pitfalls.
b: History – onset, precipitating events (trauma, drug exposure, infection), systemic symptoms.
Examination – look for discoloration, loss of sensation, pulses, abdominal tenderness, signs of SIRS.
Prioritize investigations that answer the most urgent question (e.g., is there reversible ischemia?).
If necrosis is suspected, start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics and arrange urgent imaging or surgical consult.
Document extent of necrosis to guide staging and prognosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding black discoloration of a limb with loss of sensation
Oliguria with rising creatinine >0.3 mg/dL in 48 h
High fever, hypotension, and altered mental status suggesting septic shock from necrotic infection

faq.q: How does necrosis differ from apoptosis?
faq.a: Necrosis is uncontrolled, causes membrane rupture and inflammation; apoptosis is programmed, cell fragments are phagocytosed without inflammation.

faq.q: Can necrotic tissue heal without surgery?
faq.a: Coagulative necrosis may be resorbed if small; gangrenous or infected necrosis usually requires debridement or amputation.

faq.q: Why is hyperbaric oxygen used for gas gangrene?
faq.a: It raises tissue oxygen tension, inhibiting anaerobic clostridial growth and enhancing neutrophil killing.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with a black, painless foot after a crush injury; pulses are absent. What is the next immediate step and why? — Assess limb viability, obtain Doppler, and arrange urgent surgical debridement/amputation to prevent wet gangrene and sepsis.

A patient with severe malaria develops sudden oliguria and rising creatinine. Which type of necrosis is most likely and what supportive measures are indicated? — Acute tubular necrosis; give careful fluid balance, avoid nephrotoxins, consider dialysis if refractory.

Chest X‑ray shows a cavitary lesion with an irregular wall in a HIV‑positive patient. Which necrosis pattern does this represent and what is the first‑line therapy? — Liquefactive necrosis from a bacterial/fungal lung abscess; start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) pending cultures.

A woman develops a vesicovaginal fistula after prolonged obstructed labour. Which necrosis type underlies this complication and how is it prevented? — Pressure (dry gangrenous) necrosis; prevention by timely obstetric intervention and avoiding prolonged compression.
Explain why serum LDH is often elevated in patients with extensive tissue necrosis. — LDH leaks from damaged cells; high levels indicate widespread necrosis but are non‑specific.

In a patient with suspected intestinal ischemia, what imaging finding would support liquefactive necrosis? — CT shows bowel wall thinning with gas within the wall (pneumatosis intestinalis) indicating necrotic digestion.

What distinguishes caseous necrosis on histology from coagulative necrosis? — Caseous necrosis shows amorphous, eosinophilic debris without cellular detail; coagulative retains ghost outlines of cells.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with a painful, swollen toe that becomes black and cold. What necrosis type is occurring and what urgent therapy is required? — Dry gangrenous (coagulative) necrosis; urgent re‑vascularization or surgical debridement plus pain control.
Why is it unsafe to give high‑dose aminoglycosides to a patient with existing ATN? — They exacerbate tubular necrosis, worsening renal failure.

List three systemic complications of extensive necrosis and a brief management principle for each. — Sepsis (early broad‑spectrum antibiotics, source control), electrolyte disturbances (monitor and replace potassium, phosphate), multi‑organ failure (supportive ICU care).

How does the presence of a fibrinoid necrosis help narrow the differential diagnosis? — Suggests immune‑mediated vasculitis or severe hypertension, directing work‑up toward ANA, ANCA, and blood pressure control.
